reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / international connective tissue disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Overlaps features of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and inflammatory myopathy in the same patient
High-titre anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein antibody is the defining serological hallmark
Raynaud phenomenon and puffy, swollen (sausage) hands are characteristic early features
Inflammatory myositis, arthritis, and oesophageal dysmotility are common overlapping manifestations
Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a major cause of mortality and warrants active screening
A speckled antinuclear antibody pattern with negative anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith is typical
Over time some patients evolve toward a more clearly defined single connective tissue disease
reference.pathophysiology: Mixed connective tissue disease is an autoimmune overlap disorder unified by high-titre antibodies to the U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein. Immune responses against this ribonucleoprotein complex, together with B-cell activation and immune complex formation, produce inflammation and vascular injury that combine features of lupus, scleroderma, and myositis. Proliferative vasculopathy of the pulmonary arteries underlies the characteristic pulmonary arterial hypertension, while the same immune dysregulation drives synovitis, myositis, and oesophageal dysmotility.
additionalInvestigations: Antinuclear antibody with high-titre anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein testing
Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith to help distinguish from lupus
Creatine kinase and inflammatory markers for myositis
Transthoracic echocardiography to screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT for lung involvement
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness suggesting pulmonary arterial hypertension
Severe myositis with respiratory or bulbar muscle weakness
Renal involvement raising concern for lupus-like nephritis
reference.prognosis: Many patients have a relatively favourable course with immunosuppressive control of inflammatory features, but pulmonary arterial hypertension is the principal determinant of mortality. Disease may remain stable, remit, or evolve into a defined connective tissue disorder over years.
pitfalls: Dismissing puffy hands and Raynaud as trivial and missing early disease
Failing to screen periodically for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Assuming a benign course and under-treating significant organ involvement
Overlooking evolution into lupus or systemic sclerosis during follow-up
references: Sharp diagnostic criteria and international MCTD literature
management: Suppress inflammatory features (synovitis, myositis, serositis) with corticosteroids, dosed to the severity of organ involvement
Add disease-modifying immunosuppression such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate to spare steroids and control myositis, arthritis or lung disease
Treat Raynaud phenomenon with warmth, cold avoidance and calcium-channel blockers, adding phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors or prostanoids for critical digital ischaemia
Screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension with transthoracic echocardiography and confirm by right heart catheterisation, treating with pulmonary vasodilator therapy under a specialist service
Surveil for interstitial lung disease with serial pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT, using immunosuppression for progressive disease
Relieve oesophageal dysmotility and reflux with proton pump inhibitors and prokinetic measures
Coordinate rheumatology and vascular medicine follow-up, escalating urgently for pulmonary arterial hypertension or progressive lung fibrosis
